content.title: About
content.content: Sourdough bread is a whole‑grain loaf made with a natural starter cultivated from wild yeasts and lactic‑acid bacteria. The dough rises slowly, giving the crust a crisp snap and a tangy aroma. Because of the long fermentation, it is often considered healthier than commercial yeast breads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sourdough starters have been used for over 5,000 years, dating back to ancient Egypt.
Extended fermentation increases B‑vitamins and minerals compared with standard breads.
Sourdough bread has a lower glycemic index, making it better for blood‑sugar control.
Traditional recipes require at least two days to develop a mature starter.
The acidity of the starter (pH 3.5‑4.0) inhibits pathogenic bacteria, extending shelf life.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Fermentation produces live lactic‑acid bacteria that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Lowers glycemic response
items.content: Slow breakdown of starch during fermentation leads to slower carbohydrate absorption.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Sourdough provides thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Heart‑healthy
items.content: Whole grains supply fiber, which helps reduce cholesterol levels.

items.title: Improves mineral absorption
items.content: Fermentation reduces phytic acid, allowing better uptake of iron and zinc.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Like any wheat bread, sourdough contains gluten and can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes use a noticeable amount of salt; those monitoring sodium should check the label.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The higher acidity may irritate the stomach of individuals with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread fresh, toasted, or as the base for sandwiches, soups, and salads. It pairs well with olive oil, avocado, cheese, fish, and vegetable spreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or linen sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore crust crispness.
